## New investigation idea

- **[2026-10-04] Score every paper-trading entry by its forward return, not its realized close. Turso already holds the data, and it would give the weekly strategy review a measure of edge that the capital-cap exit rule can't distort.** Today's [[finance/models/model-portfolio-management]] Strategy Performance Notes (fourth run) say again that realized A–G stats "mostly measure the 'exit the weakest P&L%' cap rule, not strategy edge": 15 of 16 paper closes since 09-01 sit at −6% to −14%. The 09-28 proposal's own caveat asks for a manual re-check of PEP/NVO/CMCSA/OTIS prices in ~60 days. The concrete step: for all ~71 paper-trading-p1 entries, compute the 20- and 60-trading-day return after entry minus SPY's over the same window, grouped by strategy, whether the position is still open or was closed. Price history is already fetched for every ticker via the existing yfinance/fetchers.py path. That gives each strategy a sample of 6–15 entries today instead of 0–10 closes, and it can't be distorted by the exit rule. It also answers the 09-28 caveat for all cut positions at once, not just four. It could be a column in `strategy_review.py` output rather than a new page. See the matching Sports Betting connection below for why this is the standard fix.


## New cross-domain connection

- **[2026-10-04] Sports Betting's bankroll stub already names the fix for the problem Finance's strategy review keeps reporting each week: Closing Line Value, a process metric that tests edge without waiting for noisy realized outcomes.** [[sports-betting/bankroll-management]] lists CLV as "the primary long-run metric" and ROI as "lagging indicator, high variance short-term". [[finance/michael-burry/burry-vs-kelly-sizing]] already says CLV "gives a direct, empirical check on whether a bettor's own edge estimate was right after the fact". Meanwhile [[finance/models/model-portfolio-management]] has now said for four weeks that paper-trading-p1's closed-trade win rates are its "ROI": small samples, dominated by an exit rule, and in B's case flipping label on a single close (10-01 favour, 10-04 in-line). The equity version of CLV is the drift of price after entry (did the market move toward your entry thesis in the next few weeks?), measured separately from when or why the position was sold. NVO is a clean example: A cut it at −11.6% on 09-28, and the Magic Formula screen re-passed it on 10-02 at a cheaper, higher-quality reading. In betting terms the line moved toward the original bet after the bettor had cashed out. This differs from the 10-02 Terrain Autobattler link, which asked for *larger samples* before acting. CLV gives *a better metric* that is usable at today's sample sizes. Sports Betting, which has no content of its own yet, would get its first worked example of CLV from Finance's own data.

## New cross-domain connections

- **[2026-10-03] AI & Tech's capex model says in writing that it has no geopolitical scenario. Today's Professor Jiang episode is the first source in the wiki that describes one: not a sudden Taiwan blockade, but a slow, lasting rise in costs as trade breaks up.** [[ai-tech/model-ai-ecosystem-constraint-edges-2026-06-27]] lists "No geopolitical disruption scenario" as its limitation #4. It treats Taiwan only as a one-off force-majeure shock and gives it no probability. The v2.1 update (2026-08-04) added three scenarios: Patel, Burry and Evans. All three are about demand or pricing, and none is about supply-chain politics. [[podcasts/podcast-diary-of-a-ceo-professor-jiang-three-predictions-collapse-world-order]] (ingested today) puts forward an "innovation equation": technological progress depends on specialisation plus globalisation, so deglobalisation slows it. That is a different risk from the one the model names. It is a gradual erosion that would make the model's three binding constraints (TSMC CoWoS in Taiwan, SK Hynix HBM in Korea, US grid queues) harder to fix with money. The model's verdict line, "Capital is not the constraint", assumes they can be fixed that way. The onshoring evidence already in AI & Tech ([[ai-tech/source-micron-us-chipmaking-2026-07-09]]) is the early, measurable form of this. Jiang's specific predictions deserve heavy scepticism, and the episode page says so itself. Even so, the model can take his channel as a fourth "Fragmentation" scenario, paired with Dalio's big-cycle framing ([[podcasts/podcast-diary-of-a-ceo-ray-dalio-i-predicted-the-2008-crash]]). It would give the model a written trigger to watch for (reshoring cost premia, export-control widening) instead of a blank.

- **[2026-10-03] Lightfin's comedy rules say what its jokes should do, but not how to write them. Today's Jimmy Carr episode is a working comedian's method for exactly that, including the "humour that faces fear" beat Lightfin needs in every episode.** [[lightfin/inspiration-authors]] sets out "two-level humour" (every set piece needs a kids' layer and an adults' layer, with Pratchett named as the systematic model) and a "warm reveal" (under the silliness, "a fear conquered"). Its only comedy material is the raw folder of Monty Python sketches and George Carlin moments: finished jokes to admire, not a way to write them. [[podcasts/podcast-what-now-with-trevor-noah-jimmy-carr-episode]] (ingested today) treats a joke as engineering: setup, misdirection, reveal, then rewrite after testing on a live audience. It also argues that dark humour is how people face what frightens them most. That makes Carr the technique to sit beside Pratchett's goal. Each two-level gag in [[lightfin/story-bible]] ("jokes for adults listening along") is one setup with two reveals, one per audience. Carr's audience-testing loop is the step Lightfin's process doesn't have. The tension worth noting is [[podcasts/podcast-diary-of-a-ceo-rick-rubin-episode]], ingested the same day, which argues for ignoring audience reaction and trusting taste. One reasonable split: Rubin for the story and the warm reveal, Carr for the individual gags.
